rv.q: The result is—how you say?—exquisite.
"English" very rightfully won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 2023, and it's hands down a masterpiece of theater.
The exquisite Broadway production from director Knud Adams is the first must-see play of the season, and its lessons are likely to stick.

Absolutely nothing gets lost in the translation of Sanaz Toossi’s English as the Pulitzer Prize-winning play about a group of Iranians longing for the West finally makes its Broadway debut, two years after its Off Broadway bow garnered critical raves and regional stagings won over audiences with its unfailing wit, grace and compassion.

Now that production, with director Knud Adams and the whole of the original cast and design team, arrives on Broadway like a welcome guest, a hopeful presence in a moment that feels like a particularly dismal party.

A delicate, buoyant comedy about a small group of adults studying the language of the title, the play disarms and delights with its depiction of ordinary Iranian citizens seeking with determination to expand the horizons of their lives.
English, Sanaz Toossi’s stunning Broadway debut, is a precise study of language’s significance.
There's a ton of intelligence at work in 'English.'
To speak in English in order to function in a new place, the play argues, forces non-native speakers to live forever in that gap.
The actual show, then, is a surprise: a gentle, subtle experience that calibrates our ears to shifts in pedagogy and understanding.
Book a ticket right now—an exquisitely written, beautifully acted and mounted one hour and forty-five minutes of theater awaits.
In any language, English is a triumph: Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer Prize-winning play is a compelling exploration of how language shapes who we are and how we navigate the world.
With its Broadway transfer, English seems to have found a universal language.
Their performances are pitch perfect, delivering beautifully nuanced portraits.
Adams is to be commended for guiding this excellent cast in doing uniformly fine work.
With empathy in short supply these days, English is a welcome reminder of what it feels like.
Because the performances are so strong, the cast members are able to mine English for every nuance of humor and individuality that is available to them.
It just doesn’t feel as deep as it did in 2022.

It is my fervent hope that English sparks curiosity for some of the Americans in the audience regarding how it would feel to migrate to a new world and prepare yourself mentally and physically to assimilate.
English is an absorbing snapshot of people in transition, seeking reinvention and self-improvement while worrying if they will shed too much of what makes them themselves.
Overall, “English” is a heartfelt, honest, and witty play.

cn.t: Toossi's Pulitzer-winning drama about Iranians learning English earns widespread praise for its smart, sensitive exploration of language and identity. Critics laud the gentle, moving storytelling and strong performances, though some find it slow-moving.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'

vr.q: I loved English I love this play it's a great play... if you love theater if you love Broadway go see this go support it

It's also incredibly heartfelt and emotional because it's not just about learning English. It's about identity and community and about how learning a new language can expand your world but also make you feel completely lost.
